P-value of the exact adaptive test

Source: R/rosenbaum-pairs.R
riposte_adaptive_pvalue.Rd

Write alpha* for the smallest level at which the adaptive test rejects the observed counts. Rosenbaum chooses the cutoffs (kB, kT) separately at each level, so the rejection regions at different levels are not always nested: counts rejected at one level can go unrejected at a larger one, and alpha* itself, reported as a p-value, would fall at or below a level more often than that level allows. The reported p-value treats alpha* as a test statistic. It is the probability, under the sensitivity bound, of counts whose smallest rejecting level is at most the observed alpha*, which is the probability of the union of the rejection regions at every level up to alpha*. It is exact at gamma = 1 and an upper bound for gamma > 1, so P(p.value <= a) <= a. When the regions are nested it is at most alpha*. Rosenbaum (2012, p. 100) reports alpha* itself as the p-value; riposte_adaptive_smallest_level() returns it.

Usage

riposte_adaptive_pvalue(y, gamma = 1, lambda = c(1/3, 2/3), scan = NULL)

Arguments

y

matched-pair differences (treated minus control). Zero differences are dropped. Ties among |y| are broken by order (ties.method = "first") with a warning, because the paper assumes untied ranks.

gamma

sensitivity parameter.

lambda

the two band fractions 0 < lambda[1] < lambda[2] <= 1 (default c(1/3, 2/3)).

scan

not used; kept so that calls written for an earlier version still run.

Value

a single p-value in (0, 1].

Details

The chance of each rejection region is computed as 1 minus the chance of the counts outside it, and that subtraction loses all its digits once the region's chance is near 1e-16. Below about 1e-15, rounding error rather than Rosenbaum's conditions decides the cutoffs. A reported p-value that small is still valid, because it is the exact chance of the region the code chose, but it should be read only as "below about 1e-15".
